title: Basic Technique
intro: Playing the guitar is two jobs: the fretting hand chooses the pitch, the picking hand starts the sound and shapes its rhythm. A few habits on each side carry you a long way.

items: Press just behind the fret (on the headstock side), not on top of it and not in the middle of the space. Less pressure is needed and the note does not buzz.
Use the fingertips, with the fingers arched so they do not mute the neighbouring strings.

Thumb behind the neck, roughly opposite the middle finger, for classical position and wide stretches; over the top of the neck for many rock and blues players, where it can also mute string 6 or fret bass notes.
One finger per fret: in a position, fingers 1–4 cover four consecutive frets. Position is named after the fret under finger 1 (fifth position: finger 1 on fret 5).

Pick (plectrum): hold it between the thumb and the side of the index finger with just the tip showing. Alternate picking (down, up, down, up) for single notes keeps the motion even; economy picking sweeps through to the next string in the same direction.

Fingerstyle: thumb (p) on the bass strings, index (i), middle (m) and ring (a) fingers on the treble strings, the PIMA naming from classical guitar. Travis picking alternates bass notes with the thumb while the fingers play a melody.

Strumming: the motion comes from the wrist and forearm, moving down and up continuously in time; the hand hits the strings on some strokes and misses on others. A common pop pattern in 4/4 is D–D U–U D U (down on 1 and 2, up on the 'and' of 2, up on the 'and' of 3, down on 4, up on its 'and').
Hammer-on: sound a note, then bring a fretting finger down hard on a higher fret to sound the higher note without picking. Pull-off: the reverse, plucking the string as the finger leaves.
Slide: move the fretting finger along the string while it sounds.

Bend: push the string sideways across the fret to raise its pitch, usually by a half or whole step, or more. A bend can stop anywhere, so guitarists play the in-between pitches of the blues (see the blues scale (#/arts/music-theory/scales-and-keys/other-scales)).
Vibrato: a rapid small bend and release, or (on classical guitar) a rocking motion along the string.

Palm muting: the side of the picking hand rests on the strings just in front of the bridge, giving a short, chunky tone. Harmonics: touch a string lightly over the 12th, 7th or 5th fret and pick it to sound the 2nd, 3rd or 4th harmonic (see The Harmonic Series (#/arts/music-theory/sound-and-pitch/harmonic-series)).

widget.title: Natural harmonics on the low E string (they sound the harmonic series)

blocks.text: Ten minutes a day of chromatic exercises (frets 1-2-3-4 on each string with alternate picking, with a metronome), chord changes between two shapes for a minute at a time, and slow scales will build accuracy faster than long irregular sessions. Increase the metronome only when the exercise is clean.

blocks.title: Harmonics
blocks.text: Touching the low E string (E2) lightly at the 7th fret gives which pitch?
solution: The 7th fret divides the string into thirds, so it sounds the 3rd harmonic: 3 × 82.4 Hz = 247.2 Hz, which is B3 (an octave and a fifth above the open string).

blocks.text: Sources: Denyer, R. (1992). The Guitar Handbook, rev. ed. Knopf; Leavitt, W. G. (1966–1971). A Modern Method for Guitar, vols. 1–3. Berklee Press; Noad, F. (2008). Solo Guitar Playing, 4th ed. Schirmer.
